title: A basket on the river
hook: Musa's mother is inspired to set her baby on the Nile, and not to fear

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Ka'ba, and a father and son asking only that their work be accepted. Your line was accept it from us. Day forty-three, and a new story: two weeks with Musa and Pharaoh.

Think of the hardest letting-go a parent ever does. The first day of school. The car keys. The airport gate. You hold on for as long as you can, and then you have to open your hands. Now make it Egypt, long ago. Pharaoh has split the land into factions, and one people, the Children of Israel, he treats as the weak ones: their baby boys are being killed. A woman among them has just given birth to a son. She's nursing him, hiding him, listening for footsteps. And then she is given an instruction that sounds like the opposite of everything a mother knows. Today: a basket on the river.

Musa, peace be upon him, is named in the Qur'an more than any other prophet, and his story comes back again and again, in pieces, across many surahs. This piece is in Surah al-Qasas, the Stories. Allah inspired the mother of Musa: nurse him. And when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear, and do not grieve. We will bring him back to you and make him one of the messengers. Look at the order. First: nurse him. Hold him while you can. Then, when the fear comes, not before: put him on the water. And then two things forbidden to her: fear and grief. Not because there's nothing to fear, but because a promise has been made, two promises, actually. He'll come back to you. And he'll be a messenger. The Qur'an calls this wahy, inspiration, the same word used for revelation to prophets, though scholars explain that for her it was a kind of inspiration placed in the heart, not prophecy. And a small surprise: the Qur'an's own word for what she used isn't basket. In Surah Ta-Ha, it's tabut, a chest or box. The basket of reeds is how Exodus tells it, and it's how many people picture it. Either way, a mother closes a lid over her baby and sets him on the Nile. Most of what we'll hear about Musa is big: fire, staffs, a sea. It begins with this: a woman opening her hands at the edge of a river, because she trusted what she had been told more than what she feared.
screen: `NURSE HIM, WHILE YOU CAN.` · `WHEN YOU FEAR, THE RIVER.` · `DO NOT FEAR, DO NOT GRIEVE.` · `NOT A BASKET — A CHEST.` · then, large: `WE WILL BRING HIM BACK TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one worry into Allah's hands, or, if that's not your language, just out of your own. Settle, and breathe. Find the worry you've been nursing, the one you keep holding close and checking on. Picture it small enough to fit in a box. Close the lid. Picture a slow, wide river, and set it on the water. Watch it drift. You're not forgetting it. You're trusting the river with it for two minutes. If you pray, you can name it as you let it go. The bell holds the time.
A basket on the river. A mother told to nurse her son, then set him on the Nile, and not to fear or grieve. Today's word.
screen: `A BASKET ON THE RIVER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: put it on the river. When the worry swims back today, picture the lid, the water, and let it float a little longer. Day forty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Musa's mother as a model of trust in Allah (tawakkul), and her story in Surah al-Qasas is often recited and taught to children.

fork.setup: you're Musa's mother. Pharaoh's men are killing baby boys. you've been inspired: nurse him, and when you fear, cast him into the river. the fear comes. what do you do?
options: hide him deeper in the house.
set him on the river, as you were told.
flee Egypt with him in the night.
fork.reveal: she set him on the Nile. with the instruction came two promises: he'll come back to you, and he'll be a messenger.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 20:39: a chest or box, the Qur'an's word for what carried baby Musa.

trapdoor: what you thought: a baby floating in a basket.
what it means: a mother told to nurse her son, then, when she feared, to set him on the river, with a promise he'd come back.
what a scholar hears: the Qur'an's word is tabut, a chest (20:39), and the word for how she was told is awhayna, from wahy, explained by scholars as inspiration in the heart, not prophecy.

sources.ref: Exodus 2:1–4 (the reed basket, named as a neighbor)

notes: The index title says 'basket'; the Qur'an's word is tabut (chest). The script keeps the title and explains the difference. A Keeper may prefer changing the title in the outline to 'A chest on the river' (separate, owner-approved edit).
'Musa is named in the Qur'an more than any other prophet' (commonly counted around 136 times). Confirm.
Wahy to Musa's mother explained as inspiration, not prophecy (the majority view; a minority of scholars discussed whether women could be prophets). Confirm framing.
Practice 'into Allah's hands' offered with an alternative for listeners who don't pray.
